title: Where are you going?
goal: Say where a trip goes to and comes from with -ra and -tik, use the short forms of joan and etorri, and buy a ticket.

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Abandoko geltokian
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to spend Saturday in Donostia and is waiting in line at the ticket office of Abando station in Bilbo.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Egun on. Donostiarako txartel bat, mesedez.
lines.id: Good morning. One ticket to Donostia, please.
lines.literal: day good. Donostia-for ticket one, please.

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.id: Round trip or one way only?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Joan-etorrikoa. Noiz irteten da hurrengo trena?
lines.id: Round trip. When does the next train leave?
lines.literal: go-come-of. when leaving is next train-the?

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.text: Hamaiketan irteten da eta ordu bata eta erdietan iristen da.
lines.id: It leaves at eleven and arrives at half past one.
lines.literal: eleven-pl-at leaving is and hour one-the and half-pl-at arriving is.

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.text: Hogeita bi euro. Bost nasatik irteten da.
lines.id: Twenty-two euros. It leaves from platform five.
lines.literal: twenty-and two euro. five platform-from leaving is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. Is the bus cheaper?

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.text: Bai, baina motelagoa. Trena azkarragoa da.
lines.id: Yes, but slower. The train is faster.
lines.literal: yes, but slow-er-the. train-the fast-er-the is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: OK, then I'll go by train.

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.id: Here's your ticket. Have a good trip!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Eta Donostiatik Bilbora, azken trena noiz da?
lines.id: And from Donostia to Bilbo, when is the last train?
lines.literal: and Donostia-from Bilbo-to, last train-the when is?

lines.speaker: Langilea:
lines.id: At ten at night. Don't miss it!

notes: **Donostiarako — the ending for a destination.** *-rako* means "for going to": a ticket **for going to** Donostia. Compare three similar forms: *Donostia**ra*** (to Donostia), *Donostia**ko*** (of/in Donostia, as a describer), *Donostia**rako*** (for Donostia, bound for Donostia).

**Trenez noa — a short form with no auxiliary.** *Joan* has a synthetic form used for a trip happening now or very soon: *noa* (I'm going), *zoaz*, *doa*, *goaz*, *zoazte*, *doaz*. The long form *joaten naiz* is for habits: *egunero lanera joaten naiz*.

**Irten and iritsi — leave and arrive.** Both take the auxiliary *izan*: *trena hamaiketan irteten **da***, *ordu batean iristen **da***. Other words you'll often see at the station: *nasa* (platform), *txartela* (ticket), *atzerapena* (delay), *aldapa*.

**Ez galdu! — a negative command.** The simplest command is just the dictionary form of the verb: *ez galdu* (don't lose/miss it), *ez ahaztu* (don't forget), *etorri hona* (come here), *entzun* (listen). More polite commands come at A2.

sections.title: To where, from where, as far as where

blocks.text: These four direction endings are one family, all built on the same place ending. If you know *etxean, etxera, etxetik*, you already have the whole system — the rest is just swapping the noun.

blocks.title: Places with irregular forms
items: *etxe* → *etxe**ra*** (to the house), but when it means "home" it's used as is: *etxera noa* (I'm going home).
*mendi* → *mendi**ra*** (to the mountains) — the sentence you'll hear most on weekends in Euskal Herria.
For people, use *-rengana*: *amarengana noa* (I'm going to Mom's). It's often used for the doctor: *medikuarengana*.

blocks.text: The two most common motion verbs have forms that stand alone, with no auxiliary. Learn them like a song — they come up in every conversation.
The prefix *ba-* adds emphasis: *banoa* ("I'm off now"), *badator* ("he's on his way"). The negative uses the same forms: *ez noa* (I'm not going), *ez dator* (she isn't coming).

blocks.title: Joan or etorri?
items: *Joan* = moving away from the speaker. *Etorri* = moving toward the speaker.

When a friend calls you from outside and you answer "I'm coming!", Basque says *banoa!* — because you're moving **away from where you are**. English says "coming" here. This flip catches many learners.
*Etorri hona* (come here), *joan hara* (go there) — two short sentences to check which one is right.

blocks.text: In Bilbo, the local train is called *Euskotren* and the city subway *Metro Bilbao*; signs are bilingual, and station names always show the Basque form first. Reading those signs is free reading practice every day — *irteera* (exit), *sarrera* (entrance), *hurrengo geltokia* (next station).
